extracted.intended_audience: General readers, researchers, journalists, and legal/education professionals interested in the Penn State/Jerry Sandusky scandal and institutional accountability
extracted.subtask_description: A comprehensive Wikipedia-style historical account of the Jerry Sandusky child-abuse scandal, subsequent investigations (Freeh report), NCAA actions, civil litigation, insurance disputes, and institutional responses at Penn State. Covers findings, sanctions, appeals, settlements, and public reaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complicity in concealing misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Freeh concluded that Paterno, Spanier, Curley and Schultz were complicit in "conceal[ing] Sandusky's activities from the Board of Trustees, the University community and authorities."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freeh's report asserts concealment as a central failure; the trustees accepted the report's conclusions and agreed to implement corrective measures. The finding was widely criticized by some reviewers and later challenged in other reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to protect children
rubrics_metrics.description: Freeh concluded that Schultz, Spanier, Curley and Paterno "failed to protect against a child sexual predator harming children for over a decade."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freeh associated this failure with institutional leadership lapses and characterized it as also constituting Clery Act violations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of empathy for victims
rubrics_metrics.description: The report said the four men "exhibited a striking lack of empathy for Sandusky's victims by failing to inquire as to their safety and well-being."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freeh used lack of inquiry into victim welfare as a moral and managerial failing supporting broader conclusions of negligence and misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowing continued, unrestricted access
rubrics_metrics.description: Freeh stated the men "empowered Sandusky to attract potential victims to the campus and football events by allowing him to have continued, unrestricted and unsupervised access to the University's facilities and affiliation with the University's prominent football program."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permitting unsupervised access to institutional facilities/affiliations for those accused of abuse was cited as an enabling factor for continued abuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to identify victim and alerting suspect
rubrics_metrics.description: The report stated the four made no effort to identify the victim of the 2001 incident, but alerted Sandusky to McQueary's allegations against him, potentially putting the victim in more danger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not identifying victims and notifying alleged perpetrators were cited as specific procedural failures exacerbating victim risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clery Act Finding #1: Clery Act violations related to the Sandusky matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Finding #1: Clery Act violations related to the Sandusky matter (proposed fine: $27,500).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of the Department of Education's proposed fines and findings assessing Penn State's compliance with the Clery Act; reflects institution-level obligations to report and respond to campus crimes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clery Act Finding #2: Lack of administrative capability
rubrics_metrics.description: Finding #2: Lack of administrative capability as a result of the University's substantial failures to comply with the Clery Act and the Drug-Free Schools and Communities Act throughout the review period, including insufficient training, support, and resources to ensure compliance (proposed fine: $27,500).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifies administrative capacity (training, resources, support) as a compliance metric under federal campus-safety laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clery Act Finding #3: Omitted/inadequate annual security/fire safety statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Finding #3: Omitted and/or inadequate annual security report and annual fire safety report policy statements (proposed fine: $37,500).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Annual security/fire safety report completeness and adequacy are explicit regulatory requirements under Clery/related regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clery Act Finding #4: Failure to issue timely warnings
rubrics_metrics.description: Finding #4: Failure to issue timely warnings in accordance with federal regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timely warning obligations are a discrete compliance duty — failure to warn the campus/public when required is a violation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clery Act Finding #5: Misclassification and nondisclosure of crime statistics
rubrics_metrics.description: Finding #5: Failure to properly classify reported incidents and disclose crime statistics from 2008–2011 (proposed fine: $2,167,500).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accurate classification and disclosure of crime statistics are core measurable obligations; large fine proposed for significant discrepancies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clery Act Finding #6: Inadequate crime-statistics collection system
rubrics_metrics.description: Finding #6: Failure to establish an adequate system for collecting crime statistics from all required sources (proposed fine: $27,500).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions must have systems to collect required crime data from all relevant sources; failure is a formal finding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clery Act Finding #7: Failure to maintain daily crime log
rubrics_metrics.description: Finding #7: Failure to maintain an accurate and complete daily crime log.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintaining an accurate daily crime log is an explicit operational requirement under campus crime reporting rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clery Act Finding #8: Reporting discrepancies between published and reported statistics
rubrics_metrics.description: Finding #8: Reporting discrepancies in crime statistics published in the annual security report and those reported to the department's campus crime statistics database (proposed fine: $27,500).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistency between published reports and official submissions is required; discrepancies can trigger fines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clery Act Finding #9: Failure to publish/distribute annual security report
rubrics_metrics.description: Finding #9: Failure to publish and distribute an annual security report in accordance with federal regulations (proposed fine: $27,500).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication/distribution timeline and content of annual security reports are regulated obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clery Act Finding #10: Failure to notify availability of reports to prospects/employees
rubrics_metrics.description: Finding #10: Failure to notify prospective students and employees of the availability of the annual security report and annual fire safety report (proposed fine: $27,500).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions must inform prospective community members about the availability of safety reports; failure is a violation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clery Act Finding #11: Failure to comply with Drug-Free Schools Act
rubrics_metrics.description: Finding #11: Failure to comply with the Drug-Free Schools and Communities Act (proposed fine: $27,500).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate statutory compliance (drug-free campus obligations) identified alongside Clery findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: NCAA standard: failure of institutional and individual integrity
rubrics_metrics.description: The NCAA characterized Spanier, Curley, Schultz and Paterno's cover-up as "a failure of institutional and individual integrity," concluding this violated basic principles of intercollegiate athletics beyond specific NCAA policies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The NCAA treated institutional integrity and adherence to core athletics principles as enforceable norms that can justify sanctions even when specific policy breaches are not the only basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: NCAA: sanctioning proportionality and consideration of collateral harm
rubrics_metrics.description: Emmert said cancelling seasons (the "death penalty") was not appropriate because it would cause "significant unintended harm to many who had nothing to do with this case," and emphasized the need to drive cultural change as well as hold the institution to account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sanctions should balance accountability with avoiding undue harm to innocent parties and aim to produce cultural/institutional reform.

rubrics_metrics.name: NCAA: death penalty reserved for repeat noncooperators
rubrics_metrics.description: In the consent decree the NCAA noted the severe "death penalty" (season cancellation) is primarily reserved for repeat violators who neither cooperated with the NCAA nor took corrective measures once the violations came to light.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cooperation and corrective measures reduce the likelihood of the harshest NCAA sanction; this is an explicit policy consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consent decree requirement: acceptance of findings and waiver of appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: The sanctions took the form of a sweeping consent decree in which Penn State accepted the findings of fact by the NCAA and waived any right to appeal the sanctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accepting a consent decree can end further appeals/investigations and is often used to obtain immediate corrective action; it also included releases for players to transfer without penalty.

rubrics_metrics.name: NCAA required remedial measures (athletics integrity/accountability conditions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Penn State was required to adopt all recommendations for reform delineated in the Freeh report; enter into an "athletics integrity agreement" with the NCAA and Big Ten; appoint a university-wide athletic compliance officer and compliance council; and accept an NCAA-appointed athletic integrity monitor for the duration of its probation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond punitive penalties, institutional accountability measures (compliance officers, monitors, required reforms) are standard remedial expectations following serious institutional failures.

rubrics_metrics.name: NCAA procedural justification for acting outside normal process
rubrics_metrics.description: The NCAA said it was compelled to act outside the normal investigative process due to what it described as the sheer egregiousness of the misconduct detailed in the Freeh report and because Penn State had commissioned the Freeh report and accepted its findings, making further proceedings redundant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extraordinary facts and an institution's acceptance of an independent investigation can justify procedural deviations by a regulator; internal emails later questioned the NCAA's jurisdiction and approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insurer limitation rationale (PMA Capital Insurance)
rubrics_metrics.description: PMA Capital Insurance Company asked the Philadelphia Court of Common Pleas to limit its exposure from a lawsuit due to both the time of coverage of the policies and possible "intentional conduct" of the university.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insurers may seek to limit coverage based on policy periods and allegations of intentional misconduct by the insured; lack of documentation by the insured can support insurer challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Settlement practice: releases of third parties
rubrics_metrics.description: The settlement agreements required victims to release several organizations, and anyone connected to them, from lawsuits, including The Second Mile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Settlement terms can include broad releases that extend beyond the direct defendant; such clauses can be controversial and may be atypical according to plaintiff attorneys.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employer liability standard (scope of employment)
rubrics_metrics.description: A U.S. District Judge ruled that Penn State could not legally be held liable for Sandusky's actions simply because he was employed there, stating that Victim 6 failed "to explain how molestation was the kind of act that Penn State employed Sandusky to perform."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To establish institutional (vicarious) liability a plaintiff must plead facts showing the tortious act was within the scope of employment or sufficiently connected to employment duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of public perception in leadership decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Frazier's stated concern was the public perception of the University's values if Coach Paterno were to remain as coach, given the seriousness of the matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public perception and institutional reputation can be an explicit factor in administrative decisions responding to serious allegations; leaders may act to preserve institutional values/credibility.
